utterances.text: And in addition to decisions on who was employed at the KP Dom, the Crisis Staff was also involved in decisions on detention and release from the KP Dom; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no room for that or need. Actually, there was no time for it because the expire date of the Crisis Staff had passed. I think you mentioned the 2nd of June. Ultimately, this tallies with the establishment of regular units and making the military structure more responsive or serious, so to say, to do away with all those who came to loot.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said previously, all of the citizens thought that it would have been better if they had not come.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Mladjenovic, there are release letters issued by the Foca Crisis Staff to KP Dom detainees, dated 7th of May, 1992, 21st of May, 1992, and 7th of July, 1992, in evidence before the Chamber. And that's P5540, P5539, and P5526. There is also a list dated the 9th of May, 1992, of people --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Actually, if we could just briefly look at this document. It's P3346.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: It says a list of people to be released without interrogation, signed by the Foca Crisis Staff. Mr. Mladjenovic, Witness KDZ239 testified before this Chamber that all those listed in this document were dead, and that's at T 18921 and 18979. In your statement, at paragraph 38, he state that with regard to the killings in the town, attempts were made to prevent them as much as possible and they were isolated individual cases. There's a wealth of evidence before this Trial Chamber of systematic killing of groups of KP Dom detainees.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: For the parties' reference, KDZ239, P3335, T 1235 to 1259, T 1265 to 1266; KDZ017's evidence, that's P56 -- sorry. P3566, at page 2387; and adjudicated facts 878 to 900. So contrary to your statement, the killings of non-Serbs in the KP Dom in Foca were not isolated incidents but, rather, they were frequent and they were systematic. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I cannot agree with that for the simple reason that it was taking place within the KP Dom with their personnel. As regards Miljevina and the people mentioned on the list, I don't know who signed it, but Miljevina is some 11 kilometres away. I didn't know about it. I wasn't familiar with it. I had no intention to say anything wrong to you or the public. Simply put, in the town where I spent the most of my time, it was not my impression that there were any mass killings there but, rather, that these were individual cases that could be investigated by experts. So individual cases. As regards Miljevina and the KP Dom when people were being brought in and taken away, it was said that they were going to be exchanged. Now whether they were or not, I can't say, because I was not a witness to it. I couldn't be in every place as physics dictates. I couldn't have been in two places at the same time. In any case, if this was confirmed through witness testimony, then it must have taken place. However, it is in the area of Miljevina which I did not visit in the war much. The road could only be used in 1993 to travel between Foca, Trnovo and Sarajevo. That was in 1993, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mladjenovic. And thank you for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you for your indulgence in relation to the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mladjenovic, on page 48, you said if this was confirmed by witness testimony, then it must have happened. Does it mean that we accept that the witness in question told the truth?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a bit -- that's the big question. I'm trying to testify here fairly and honestly. That was my intention. Indeed, it could happen that the person in question was not honest. It happened that Muslims who reported a victim, then appear at elections as was the case in many locations throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina. So this doesn't need to be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the document back, P3346.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was suggested to you that the decision to release these people was made by the Crisis Staff of Foca. Please read out aloud the first sentence underneath the title which says "list."

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Pursuant to a request of the Miljevina Territorial Defence and the approval of the 7th Battalion Command, the following persons shall be released without interrogation." You are correct, Mr. Karadzic. It doesn't say the Crisis Staff. It says the 7th Battalion Command and Miljevina. I'm surprised to see that they were released without any interrogation. I don't know what it was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us this, please, did they ask for it or request? What is the third word? Did they demand it or ask for it?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Pursuant to a request of the Miljevina Territorial Defence and the approval of the 7th Battalion Command, the following persons shall be released without interrogation."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, this is nothing to do with the witness. It has to do with interpretation. It has to be interpreted by "demand," rather than "request."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It is our professional assessment as stated in the interpretation. Mr. Karadzic can request clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I think a word -- is a word missing from the English translation? Mr. Mladjenovic, could you kindly read out the sentence which appears below "the list."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, above "the list." So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Above "the list": "Pursuant to a request by the Miljevina Territorial Defence and the approval of the 7th Battalion Command, the following persons shall be released without an interrogation." And then we have a list of 18 people, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I note that the "request" is missing from the English translation. You confirm that, Ms. McKenna?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I've also observed that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we proceed?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But the word "zahtjeva" is still in question. The Territorial Defence cannot request. Can we have that clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How would you translate "pursuant to their asking for"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, if you have problem -- issue with the translation of this word "zahtjeva" you may request officially to the CLSS in writing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But I'd like to ask the witness whether there's a difference between "zahtjev" [phoen] and "tranzinje" [phoen].

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. But the sheer nature of things, the two words exist due to their difference in meaning and not ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that, at the outset, the KP Dom prison was under the civilian authorities. What happened with the people after interrogations? What was the outcome of such interrogations?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that, at the beginning of the war, it was never under the civilian authorities. It was under the military component, which, at the time, first, was the units of the TO, and then in May, on the 12th, regular units were established. By virtue of that, the civilian authorities lost any competence. It was converted to a military prison. Indeed, during their -- during the withdrawal, the Muslims entered there as the prison is situated in the settlement mostly populated by Muslims. And then they moved onto Gorazde, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But before the 12th of May, before a decision was made to establish the army, you said it was the Crisis Staff had authority before the army was established. Can you tell us whether people were released after interrogation? Were some released after interrogation? What happened with one group and what with the other? What effect did it have?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say this: Before my departure, I asked one of the military officers whom I held in high regard -- in one go, there were 64 persons who obviously could not have been engaged by the military, Muslim military. According to his words, the 64 persons were released. They were Muslims. That was right after the take-over when the KP Dom was taken up by the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 16752, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know Pilav, Hasan Pilav?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hasan Pilav. I knew him. He was an agricultural engineer by profession. I was his son's teacher in high school. He worked in the public utility company for roads, and before that in the Zelen Gora company. I knew also knew another physician from the Pilav family, and one of their members was also a TO staff head and he was much discussed. That's as far as my knowledge goes regarding that family.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at this. This is before the 12th of May. That is to say, the 26th of April. This man was captured in combat operations. And was released from the Foca penal and correctional facility because after the informative processing he was supposed to report to the police station. Was this standard treatment in terms of those who were not prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. The 64 people, due to their age, and probably the same goes for Mr. Hasan, because I see he was born in 1938 and he was not a military conscript by that time, so they were treated the same way probably. Interrogated first. But I don't know why criminal reports were not submitted, if they could be proven. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this document admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3318, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now I would like to see 1D1688. This is a Defence exhibit. I would like to see it briefly. No, that's not that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have number 1 before D?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. D1688. The document should have been admitted. That's why I said that this was a Defence exhibit which has been admitted. Now we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you comment upon this document? What is it about? Who was in charge of releasing people on the 18th of July, 1992? Who was the one who did the screening and decided on their release?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The signatory is the commander of the tactic group, Mr. -- Colonel Marko Kovac. It says here that Mirsad Alic is hereby being released from prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The check has been -- that Alic did not have any participation -- participation, did not take part in such dealings and is therefore released into Foca: "A check has been carried out by competent organs into the work and impact of enemy activity in Foca."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How does this tally with what you know about the screening procedures and decisions as to who would be prosecuted and who would be released? How does this tally -- or, rather, how does this conform with what you knew, not about this particular individual, but about the whole phenomenon?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I did not really keep abreast. I don't know whether this happened frequently. This is a military story. This is military conduct. I did not get involved in that. I don't know how commonplace that was. Believe me, I can't confirm anything here. Although, the Prosecutor also asked me about a case, or perhaps two, a person was processed and let go. The person was released based on the information that he had not taken part in any crimes; for example, the arming activities, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is Mirsad Alic's ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose he is Muslim. You can tell, of course. You can tell by his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We know, we can tell, but the other participants do not hail from the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but we know how to tell each other apart by our first and last names. Unfortunately, the roots of that should be studied. It's an entirely different story.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 45, Ms. McKenna suggested that you wrote something in P3340 -- or, rather, that you acted on behalf of the Crisis Staff with regard to work obligation. However, in that paper, it says the Executive Board and you signed your name as the president of the Executive Board there. Was that within the purview of the Executive Board? Did you issue that order on behalf of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's be clear on one thing immediately. I didn't notice that, to be honest. I didn't notice whether I signed that or not. But never or rarely did I sign on behalf of the Crisis Staff, but I did sign on behalf of the Executive Board. On the composition of the Executive Board, there was Milica Miletic [phoen], who was a new member, and he was also the head of the military department who was in charge of mobilisation and all the other such activities. That department was in charge of those activities. Therefore, although I signed the document that would have been done on behalf of the collective body that was in charge of that but that concerned the sentry service that was about pulling out people who were not militarily able-bodied men or did not belong to the units or who worked in the KP Dom or perhaps were not even guards there but worked on other things, and they were of ill health, for example, so we wanted to have them at least the sentry duty. They wanted them to be nominated on the request of Mr. Karac [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber briefly what is war obligation; who is subjected to that? And what is work obligation; who is subject to that?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The so-called war obligation concerns the military component. And this is established by the act of mobilisation. We are talking about people who are under 65 years of ages, who are healthy, who had served in the army previously and who are on the records of the military department. And now, the work obligation - and I subscribed to that from the very beginning, from the 19th - that concerns work in those bodies in companies, in the outpatients' clinic or hospital, and other such institutions. All the perks that were enjoyed by the soldiers, by the military component, did not pertain to people who were under work obligation. For example, they had double years of seniority and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In terms of ethnic affiliation, who was subjected to work obligation? Was a distinction made there at all?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to work obligation, we made sure that we also called those people who were necessary. For example, a colleague of mine, my school buddy Mustafa Smajovic [phoen] was supposed to be engaged as well as a woman who was from a mixed marriage. And there was a woman who was supposed to work in a company. She was Muslim -- the wife of an officer. So, of course, since the requirements were reduced for personnel in the municipality, I engaged perhaps only five or six clerks in the municipality. And the rest, if they were able-bodied men, were sent to the front line to be engaged in combat there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 36, lines 16, to -- the question about punishment, i.e., that -- those who Miroslav Stanic praised they were not punished. You say that they couldn't be punished, why? Can you tell us why?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could not be punished because they, at that time, acted in concert with the regular units of the army and they represented a component which meant a lot at that time. The second reason is that some of them -- I didn't agree, I would never agree with that assertion and that was a part of the package deal. If some of them committed, and it was proven that they were involved in some dodgy deals and then they were convicted. They were found guilty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 37, within the same context, you were asked why Radovan Stankovic asked to be transferred from the military into the police. And bearing in mind both of these examples, can you tell us when did you learn about that. What did you know about the time, about the things for which they were subsequently charged?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can -- I have to tell you honestly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Just before the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Just before the witness answers. Mr. Karadzic has stated that Mr. Mladjenovic was asked why Radovan Stankovic asked to be transferred from the military into the police. That's incorrect. That wasn't asked of Mr. Mladjenovic. Perhaps it's a transcript issue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a transcript issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were asked about a list with Radovan Stankovic featuring in the place. My question is this: What did you know at the time and what could I know about the accusations subsequently raised against them.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it tell you that I paid attention only to number 1. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I don't think it's a correct question to ask the witness what Mr. Karadzic knew at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. It is I who he is asking, if I understood things correctly. I'm supposed to answer; right? I believe that Mr. Karadzic asked me what I knew about Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. McKenna. Do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the way I understood the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think witness is correct in so understanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: If the question is simply what the witness knew about Stankovic, of course, there is no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh. Just a second. But also -- I missed this part. What could I know about the -- [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: It's at line 18 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's not an appropriate answer -- question for the witness. Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as Mr. Stankovic is concerned, I was disappointed when I learnt, but I did not know anything about that during the proposition phase, the suggestion phase. I didn't participate in that. I knew him as my fellow citizen, as a lad. He was rather robust and a nice fellow. I didn't know that he was engaged in those activities that he was convicted for. How did he end up on the list for the special police? Somebody had to serve that for approval to the ministry or to some other structure - I don't know which. I suppose it would be the ministry - for his presence to be approved. Obviously with hindsight I would certainly never have approved that. I'm sure that Karadzic would not either, or the ministry, or the minister himself. Nobody would have approved such appointment. But that's with hindsight, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On line [as interpreted] 5 of today's transcript, you said that the mandate of the Territorial Defence commander expired in 1998. I believe that this should be correct. When did his mandate expire?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have misspoken. It was on the 6th of May, 1898.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the transcript. Look at what is on the screen. Look at the screen. It's the nineteenth century?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, 1989 [Realtime transcript read in error "1998"].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I didn't mean to -- therefore -- one gets tired and attention wanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Again this was misrecorded. You said "1989," right?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 6th of May, 1989. It is my religious holiday. But he remained the TO commander until the very -- very end. It was a body which comprised both Serbs and Muslims until the end of the war. At the same time, did he -- he discharge you as the president of the Crisis Staff, they told us that painstakingly, and some other persons whom we only guessed about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just as Ms. McKenna asked you, could you please provide the shortest answers possible. In -- in P6265, there is a reference to mopping up of Foca but that was not completed. What does that term mean in military terms? Who is Foca mopping up --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, the term "mopping up" was used so it may be construed differently.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Mopping up" is a military term. It's sanitation of the area. For example, you can sanitise the area from mines from and explosives, so this is the term that should be used, "sanitisation." I apologise, what else did you ask me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does that include removing civilians from the area?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to the movement of civilians, I have to say that this will require me to go to a somewhat greater length, but it will not go amiss, I'm sure. According to my statement and some other documents the media did their bit, and in addition to sowing hatred among the two people, they also saw -- sowed fear, and the ground was very fertile because in the two world wars, the First World War and the Second World War, the Muslims and the Serbs also suffered trauma and remained --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I think we heard enough. I don't think we heard the word "mopping up" in Exhibit P6265. I rarely do intervene, but how much more do you need for your conclusion? Today we need to rise exactly at 2.45, and bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If our lunch break is at customary time, at half past 12.00, I will finish before the break --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm referring to the next witness, whether we can finish him by the end of today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think we if we start at the beginning of the next session since you have an allotted one hour for cross-examination, we can finish him, but it will be close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking whether he can conclude as soon as possible. Yes, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Excellencies, in this document, P6265, in the English translation, this word "ciscenje" was translated as "mopping up."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is P6265 not the interview of Ostojic? Where he said Foca was run by the Crisis Staff. I think the saw the mopping up in the P3544 where the Zaga detachments were referred to, but I may have been mistaken. But --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right. You are probably right. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mladjenovic, in the questions she put to you, Ms. McKenna repeated this suggestion of taking over power. Can you tell us who was in power in Foca? Before the war, during these events, and during the war.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, at the multi-party elections --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please just keep it short, if possible.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslims and Serbs. Possibly there might have been some Montenegrins or perhaps Croats. Montenegrins were not a constituent people but personnel solutions like that could be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In line 15 - thank you - you said that you filled the positions that had previously been held by the Muslims in the Executive Board. The Muslim side, did they have, in accordance with the agreement reached, the right to have their own municipality and their own Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could have, had agreement been reached, of course, as they have now. Indeed, things have changed now because there are different institutions and a president of the municipality. However, the executive branch remained the same, the departments, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Help us with this: On the 8th or 9th, or any time in April, did you take over power in Foca and if so from whom?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No way. Civilian authorities, indeed, we met on the 15th, when we appointed some other persons as acting officer holders who were supposed to keep an eye on property of companies so that the police could secure peace throughout the town itself and possibly in the villages too. So, on the 19th of April, I came to the municipality with my co-workers, this was a small number of people, and they were immediately involved in work obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned in line 19 your co-workers, Edhim [phoen] and others. Can you tell the Chamber what their ethnic background is?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three of them were ethnic Muslims: Aganovic, Edhim Varajic [phoen], and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lojo?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, Taib Lojo was present in the municipality. So Aganovic, and Senad, I think I have forgotten the name, who was head of finance. And on the other side there were three Lakovic, Bodiro [phoen], Gavojislav [phoen] and I as the president. Taib Lojo was president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Mr. Karadzic's microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 13, and more frequently in that segment, on that topic, it was persistently suggested that the municipality, the Serb municipality of Foca, was established on the basis of some instruction that had arrived from me. And on page 14, you said that this was a recommendation. D1183 is the document that I'd like us to take a look at now. I'd like to ask you whether that is what you meant. So it's a Defence document, 1183.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Just that -- excuse me, before --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Before we show the witness the document, Mr. Karadzic might want to lay a foundation. Otherwise, he will be leading with the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He was asking whether this is the document he referred to. Is it leading? We'll allow the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mladjenovic, please, take a look at what is says here: "Recommendation, 15th of January, 1992." And that's the Official Gazette. And look at the date, please. And who sent this recommendation on the establishment of assemblies of municipalities of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Could we please zoom in on this.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that. It was signed. This recommendation was signed by the president of the Assembly of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik, master of sciences. Yes, you can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When was this session of the assembly held?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 11th of December, 1991, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it suggested to you that this recommendation was based on some meeting that was held on the 19th of December?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say with any certainty before I look at the document. But, quite certainly, on the basis of this recommendation, on the 25th of December, 1991, we established -- well, to play it safe, not to be unprepared, if there is this disaster of conflict. On the 15th of March, we held a joint session, in 1992, and I remember that we stopped halfway, and we did not meet again, all of us together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell us precisely which recommendation you followed, the recommendation I sent or the one that you see before you?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Momcilo Krajisnik's recommendation. He was president of the assembly, so it is analogous that the president of the assembly can make a recommendation to the president of the assembly --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not catch the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who was elected, proposed, 25th of December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Executive Board went on working together with the Muslims until the 8th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. It's ... I will read out your answer as reflected in the transcript, and please correct me or supplement what is missing: "Momcilo Krajisnik's recommendation." It is answer to the question from Mr. Karadzic: "Tell us precisely which recommendation you followed ..." "Momcilo Krajisnik's recommendation. He was the president of the assembly so it is," somebody, "that the president of the assembly can make a recommendation to the president of the assembly." So that part is not clear. Could you repeat that Mr. Mladjenovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to tell you that in this last part -- oh, yes, I see, this is zoomed in, this recommendation. I really haven't read it but I know the essence, because action was taken on the basis of his recommendation that at the level of municipality --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot see where the witness is reading from. Very fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mladjenovic, did you hear my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My understanding was that this is a recommendation that we received from the president of the assembly of the Serb People in BH, Momcilo Krajisnik. The 11th of December, 1991. Whether there were any other ones, I really don't know. It is quite possible, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, let's continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think that His Excellency Kwon asked you what the connections were between the Assembly of the Republic and the Assembly of the municipality. Can you tell us who was in charge of the Assembly from central level and who was in charge of the Executive Board from central level?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we look at this from the point of view of substance, the Assembly of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was in charge of passing laws, resolutions, and such enactments. And at lower level, that is to say, at levels of municipalities, these laws are brought down to the level, if I can put that way, of decisions, conclusions, and so on, and these are the usual type of enactments at this lower level, lower than the republican assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the republican parliament to municipal parliament --

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Executive Board prepares these decisions or resolutions for the assembly of the local parliament, the local assembly. Adjusts them, prepares them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P3333; could we have a look at that now, please. Uh-huh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, can you take a look, the Official Gazette of the Serb municipality of Foca, you passed this decision on the establishment of the municipality. Or, actually, the Assembly of the Serb municipality. Article 4 reads as follows: "Members of the assembly of the Serb People of the Municipality of Foca will continue working and all working bodies," et cetera et cetera? Could you tell me what the difference is between the establishment of a municipality and the Assembly of the Serb People in a territorial sense?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assembly is an organ that is elected according to inertia, when Serb MPs were outvoted in the People's Assembly of BH and then, just in case so as not to be taken aback, the Assembly of the Serb People was established, and it included assemblymen who were elected at the elections, mostly from the SDS and Durakovic's Communists, two or three, I think, then Ante Markovic's reformists. These were the structures that comprised this assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you just explain the substance of Article 5?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the next page in English now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The Assembly of the Serb People in the municipality of Foca recognises the validity of documents issued by the Assembly of the Municipality of Foca, unless they run counter to the interests of the Serb people." That is what Article 5 says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that that was written in the recommendation as well, the one that we had in the previous document? The same wording was there as well?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. I didn't really pay attention.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the text that Mr. Karadzic is reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just -- what are you reading from?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The previous document, the recommendation. I would like to indicate that Article 5 reflects the first paragraph of the recommendation and its essence. Actually, I can deal with that in my final submissions too. Is it break time now, Excellency?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can continue, if necessary. I'd like you to conclude your re-examination. Then we'll have a break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to show something from the video so I'll need at least 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh. Then we'll have a break. We'll have a break for 45 minutes and resume at quarter past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.31 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at 65 ter 11021.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were shown the minutes or, actually, the transcript, and we could hear you speak at the SDS meeting of the 14th of February. I wanted to ask you - well, can we have page 9, please - so that can you explain to us what you had in mind when you said that. Page 9. Can we zoom in, please. I will read it out: "Secondly, as regards the other questions that need to be defined and ultimately make the Serbian municipality functional, I don't think it was discussed here." What did you mean when you said ultimately there may be a necessity to make the Serbian municipality into operation?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the context was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When was it established; and when did it become operational?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was established on the 25th of December, 1991, and it became operational, I think, officially, it started working after the dissolution by the commissioner. I think it was in September that it began working in full capacity.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because there was a dissolvement, then for a while we did not meet, and all of the work had to be done by the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Further below, you complain that in terms of the TO and the staffing, there seems to be something wrong. I wanted to read out the MUP part. Is the identical situation with the MUP. The regional centre of Gorazde, the place which belonged to the state security and the SDS almost saw a Muslim being promoted and appointed. Please, people, who is dealing with this and what is being done? Can you tell us what this is about and what does it have to do with the establishment of Serb institutions?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those persistent avoidance to implement the agreements that were signed, and it was avoided by relevant Muslim representatives to honour their agreement with the Serbian side. The magical Territorial Defence Staff, existed practically up until the war, and at its helm was someone whose term of office was expired. It was done also in the centre for state security and some other positions that had been agreed upon and signed. Unfortunately, that is why I expressed my concern, asking what was it that you people were doing there, and I had in mind certain officials who were higher up the hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this page, although partially it has been admitted. In the English language, this is not the correct one, and the Defence will shortly inform you of the appropriate page. It is page 9 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I think it's page 13 in the English, if that assists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you know what the previous exhibit number is?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6264, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we add this part to the exhibit? Shall we do that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll add this page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we next have 65 ter 40609. That was the interview we partly heard. Can we also have the transcript? It is -- it is 40609, and the other one is [In English] D00007261A, [Interpretation] the recording. Can we have page 2 of the transcript on the display for the participants? Can we play from 7 minutes and 50 seconds to 8 minutes and 42 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have that entire transcript. It will be impossible to interpret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note it. I take it you didn't circulate the translate to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm told that we did, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I heard they don't have it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can we please have an exact reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you tell us where it is again?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 2, the bottom. "VO, Foca is one of the ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's try.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 7 minutes 50 to 8 minutes 42. Can we hear it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Foca is one of the points in the territory of former Bosnia-Herzegovina with terrible conflicts between Serb Orthodox Christian and Muslim population broke out for the simple reason that Muslims had envisaged Foca to be a European Islamic cultural centre, and in town the Serb population were the majority and because, on April the 8th, last year, a group of Mujahedin and local Muslims in Foca wanted to kill respectful Serbs in this town. That is how the war started on the religious basis in Foca."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The words of the late Mr. Ostojic, how true are they, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the month of April and the establishment of units, I can confirm that, I can confirm that there -- as regards the presence of the Mujahedin, in that context and in that period, I did not pay much attention to it, although I did have certain knowledge. I was threatened in 1991, and I was on a list. Now whether those were the Mujahedin or some other radical currents in their policy, that's something I don't know. But I did mention the flyers distributed by Mr. Sabanovic at the rally in Foca in 1992 in terms of how Serbs were to be treated. It is quite an ugly document, unfortunately, and I have it with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you about that. In other words there were lists of prominent Serbs to be liquidated?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was one of them. Perhaps the first one on the list. There were others too. It probably is somewhere in the documents. I didn't pay much attention to it, because, well, what could I do?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we next hearing something from page 3. It is the second paragraph from the top, which is 9 minutes 6 seconds to 9 minutes 45 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "I claim with full responsibility that civilian population in Foca, both Serb and Muslim, remained intact. And that in fact the first clashes were between the armed groups, the Mujahedin and local Muslims, who wanted to conquer the town and turn it into a prison, similar to Gorazde. But the Serb population resisted and liquidated those armed groups and made it possible for the Muslim civilians to withdraw in the direction of Gorazde and Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that Foca, as a town, had a majority Serb population?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As per the 1991 census, well, I have to say that it was never verified by the People's Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but it is an application even nowadays. Since the town is on both sides of the Cehotina and the Drina, in any case the population was predominantly Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true what Mr. Ostojic says that they attacked Foca trying to seize control?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was indeed an attack on Foca executed by the Muslim forces from Sukovac and that other hill Siriste [phoen]. They used mortars, as far as I know, and the launcher that produced terrifying sound that probably scared both Muslims and Serbs. They were targeting our Crisis Staff, which was in the direction of the church.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to confirm whether it was true what is stated. Now as for what is said about the civilians, that both Serb and Muslim civilians remained intact in the first clashes of the armed groups.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the course of those first few day, definitely so. I have to say that around the 10th or so, perhaps later, a Muslim soldier was killed, three Serb soldiers were killed, and a KP Dom inmate who was standing by obviously.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Who was a bystander.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is why we established a commission, comprising Dr. Zijo Ajanovic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the names. We didn't catch them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mladjenovic, could you repeat your answer from -- after you said, "... three Serb soldiers were killed ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two in Aladza. If there is any need, I can comment on it further. I attended the funeral because they could not be buried in the town. They were buried in a nearby village. On behalf of the Crisis Staff, I was tasked with going there. There was also a KP Dom inmate. The story was that he was supposed to throw a hand-grenade on our soldiers, but it exploded in his hand. There was another soldier who was killed on a nearby hill where the main clash between the Serb and Muslim side occurred. It was at the very beginning, on the 8th and the 9th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's be brief. When you say a joint commission, you mentioned some names. Please always tell us what you mean when you say a joint commission, in terms of ethnicity. And also when you say the names, could you please specify their ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note the witness needs to re-start his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You started answering the question while we are hearing the interpretation of Mr. Karadzic's question. So could you put a pause. And please start over again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologies. As regards the commission, when I say a joint or a mixed commission, it comprised the following physicians: Dr. Zijo Ajanovic, neuropsychiatrist; Cedo Skipina, judge; and Dr. Maric Junior, Radmilo, that is. They worked for a few days, perhaps seven or eight days. They carried out an on-site investigation at the foot of Celovina hill and in Djedjevo village where the clashes were. I think there were 14 casualties, and their report confirmed that they were killed in a clash.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Zijo Ajanovic, what is his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim. I believe I said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was not recorded because of the overlap. In the excerpt, late Mr. Ostojic says that it was made possible for the Muslim civilians to withdraw to Gorazde and Sarajevo. Were these civilians driven away, driven out, or were they enabled to leave?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, no one drove them away. There was no opportunity to do so. They were withdrawing when the separation line was near the health centre. I kindly ask you for your patience. What did the media do? Mr. Semsko Tusakovic [phoen], Radio Sarajevo journalist, announced the arrival of Serbo Chetniks from Serbia and Montenegro. He said there were 4- or 5.000 of them and it scared everyone, Serbs and Muslims. He even used that figure when at Ustikolina there were Muslim units present. That is why the population was afraid, having the experience of the previous wars, and they withdrew in the evening and during the night. Donje Polje and most of the centre of town withdrew in that way, in their vehicles, and on foot. The other part withdrew to Pluzine. It included Serbs and Montenegrins and Muslims. So the figure was around 2300 not all at once, but in different periods. They went to their friends because they expected the conflict to last for a short time only and that a solution would be found. It is also interesting to note that when the Muslims turned to the SUP, requesting -- and to the civilian authorities, requesting that they be allowed to leave, they -- we had to consult the military structures because pressure was brought to bear on me, in particular, when it was said that we are waging war whether it is Radojica and his civilian structures are bussing them here and there. They expressed their wish to the MUP to leave collectively and it was probably for safety reasons that they opted for that, saying that they wanted to go to Serbia, Montenegro, and Macedonia. No one asked to go to Gorazde or Sarajevo, and that can be checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us briefly what is the faith and ethnicity of their friends in Pluzine where some 2300 Muslims from Foca took shelter?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't only the Muslims. The first wave of population withdrawal included Muslims, Serbs, and Montenegrins. Well, for Montenegrins, it may have seemed natural because they were, they were the so-called Pivljani, were employed in Foca working in the town hospital and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Karadzic kindly repeat his answer [sic].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I am grateful to you for being so extensive, but I'd just like you to tell us what the religion was of their friends in Pluzine where they sought shelter?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Orthodox.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to remind the participants -- actually, let me just ask this. Did you have a situation in which you prevented people from leaving and then did you lift that ban? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that happened too. I -- actually, in my building, on the floor where I lived, in different apartments, of course, there were some that were owned by Muslims. There were over 30 people staying there. Serbs gave me trouble too. They were saying the president is protecting them, and so on and so forth, when the situation became unbearable. Actually, I also had a friend from school there and I advised her that they should go somewhere more peaceful so they could survive. And to tell you the truth, they grabbed the chance. They went to the MUP. They announced their departure, and they were transported by bus to destinations in Serbia, Macedonia and Montenegro, Skopje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The lady who went to school with you, what was her ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was a Muslim. She had two children. She lived one floor above me. Otherwise she worked at the court there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: P2642. That's what I'm going to read out to you, or, rather, just one sentence, "The decision is from the 18th of June, 1992" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: This is too fast to follow what is being read out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I identified the document. It is a document of the War Commissioner of the Serb municipality. It's sent to the operative staff and the Executive Board of the Serb municipality of Foca. The third paragraph says --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please read slow. Very slow. Slowly when the interpreters do not have the documents. Shall we switch to the e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P -- it's a Prosecution Exhibit. P2642.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are waiting, Mr. Karadzic, do you like to tender or add the clip and transcript of Ostojic to the previous exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The previous one was a Prosecution document. All right. But finally I do have a few more excerpts. We'll go back to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now I don't want to us read out all of this but please look at the beginning of the third paragraph, the current civilian and military authorities of the Serb municipality of Foca have so far prohibited both Serbs and Muslims from leaving the territory of Foca. And then the War Commission suggests the following: "The civilian and military authorities shall allow all loyal citizens who have no violated laws to leave," and so on. And paragraph 3 midway it says, "to compile lists with all necessary data of those loyal citizen who have expressed a wish to leave, who are to be informed of this decision and who are to give a short signed explanation of their reasons for leaving the municipality." And now can we have the next page in Serbian. This is number 5: "The Executive Board should compile a list of the property that remained in Foca, meaning the property that could not be transported under current conditions." So can you tell us whether people were being chased away or whether you had actually prohibited them from leaving at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was prohibited both for Serbs and Muslims. Serbs, even military conscripts, intended to leave, to take their families away, and this pertained to Serbs, and this could have been considered military desertion because they were military conscripts. Of course, I have another statement too that was signed by the president of the municipal assembly to return to the situation the 5th of April, 1992. And it says --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It is being read out too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you concentrate on answering the question. If necessary, Mr. Karadzic will ask further questions. And if you are reading a document, please read very slowly for the benefit of interpreters. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to ask whether there was a ban and whether the Executive Board, as Article 5 says, registered property and tried to protect the property that they could not transport at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilian authorities, that is to say the Executive Board, tried, and I mean -- well, they did this paperwork, stating that entry was prohibited into all apartments and houses and this was supposed to be ensured by the civilian police and the military. I already said that at first the results were good, but, later, on -- how do I put this? This, in other words, well, it -- they had to rely on neighbours and other people to take care of their houses. If they decided to leave, then a Serb would take over -- no, not take over. To have the keys and, in that way, a neighbour would take care of his neighbour's apartment or house. This would have to be a longer story. But I hope that you see what the essence is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That will do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go back to the interview, 07261/2 and the transcript is 40609. Number 3 -- no, it's on the fourth page. 13 minutes, 29 seconds, up to 14:01. In the transcript, it is page 4. 40609 is the 65 ter number of the transcript. And the video ... oh, we don't have to listen to it. All right. Let us look at the transcript. It's the third paragraph. I'm going to read it out now in the English language. Oh, we are going to play it after all, yes. 13:29 to 14:01 and the transcript can be followed on page 4.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "I do not have that information. I think that did not happen, and from the very beginning of the war and conflict in Foca and the International Red Cross and UNPROFOR were there. And, as far as I know, all detained Muslims in the Foca prison have been exchanged in the meantime and these are extremists who had started the armed struggle against the Serb people in the territory of Foca."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What can you say with regard to the accuracy of this statement of Ostojic's, in the briefest possible terms?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as this, that they were exchanged, they were every now and then. Not all of them. I wouldn't agree with that. And what would happen was that people would go for an exchange and then I remember that they were even brought to Kula and then they waited for a few months to be exchanged. I remember Dr. Selimovic, Dr. Karovic, and others and their turn came only -- well, I don't know whether they had not reached agreement with the Muslim side. Believe me, I don't know. But -- but I do know that they went out for an exchange as did many others, but, on the whole, I'm not sure that I would agree with the statement. So, in part, yes. But in its entirety, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the Red Cross have access? Did UNPROFOR have access to Foca?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The International Red Cross did. I think that UNPROFOR did too. Believe me -- well, the International Red Cross, yes, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A list had been compiled. As for the numbers, I didn't go into that. I didn't have the opportunity of looking at these lists. It would be a good thing to consult the International Red Cross, and, of course, institutions that entered the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now hear the next answer. That is also on page 4 from 14:17 to 14:45.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "However, a certain practice was discovered both with the Muslim and Croatian authorities which is this: When they cannot explain a large number of casualties an armed clashes with the Serbs, then they justify it by telling families and the international community that they had perished in Serb prisons. By the way, I myself have never been in the Foca prison."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there manipulations in your experience that sometimes people would be reported as civilians and sometimes as combatants and --

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the practice, for sure. And not only at this location, but also in other places. Many things were hyperbolised. These are Muslims who were well known. Why they did that, I don't know, maybe to justify their objectives. Quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 5 in the transcript, can we play 15:45 to 16:09. I skipped some. So from 15:46 to 16:09, so the transcript page is 5 from the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Let those facts be established as well. If something like that happened, I have nothing against it. I'm not defending individual crimes, and I am not defending anything that could have happened out of control of both state authorities and the regular army because the dirtiest of all wars is being waged in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that is a religious war."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did the authorities contribute to the commission of crimes? Did they encourage them or did they hide them in Foca?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. From the level of the republican authorities or the local level, absolutely the situation was not being exacerbated and, of course, it was not being suggested to anyone that they should commit crimes. I absolutely assert that. Except for exceptions. Of course, there were exceptions. But at the level of the town, it's a lot if one person falls victim. Let me tell you that straight away. I would agree with that. But there wasn't any major victimisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What did you say about the republican level? It wasn't recorded.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such orders did not arrive from republican level either. I know that in Foca 551 civilian --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please repeat the numbers slowly and the references.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you -- could you repeat your answer again. And very slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, as far as the Serb side is concerned, in the conflict, throughout the war, 551 soldiers lost their lives, 95 civilians -- so the total was 646. I would like the Muslim side to present sincerely and reliably the losses. The loss of a single life is a loss for all, for humankind, and that is how I view that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 25:36 to 36 [as interpreted] transcript page 7. So could we have that played, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot find the reference on this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Should we play this part again. Could you give the reference to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The third paragraph on page 7. And then it's the middle of the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Accepting this story. In every war, there are crimes that are really crimes, and neither state authority nor its institutions are behind it, and they should be looked into and sanctioned. But to build an attitude towards one people on an account of individual cases is really immoral and impermissible."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This presented position of Mr. Ostojic's, how does that tally with your own experience in terms of the position of state organs and local organs in respect of crimes?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite certainly, I share the position of the late Mr. Ostojic. Namely, that all of those who committed crimes, this is a personal act, and they should be held responsible for the judiciary organs unequivocally, regardless of nations or nationality involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I would like to tender all the transcripts of what we have played. You can add a D or a P, whichever you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honours, given the extensive Defence reliance on this, I suggest tendering the transcript in its entirety. It will make the record clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it in its entirety. So that -- so Exhibit P -- what is --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6265, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yeah, will be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 40609.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said earlier today that on the 8th, you reached an agreement with the leadership of the Muslim community and that, at the same time, or immediately thereafter, fire was opened, an attack was carried out; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. That's what I said. While I was in the municipality with my associates, because we had agreed to meet there and to make another effort towards co-ordinating our positions, we spoke on the telephone, and very simply, fire was opened from the Muslim side. There was a response from the Serb side. On our way back, or, rather, when decided to say our good byes and I suppose that everybody went to their own Crisis Staff. I suppose they did. I did. I went with Mr. Markovic. The town was empty. The main streets were absolutely empty. The town was a ghost town. There was nobody.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] can we look at 65 ter 1501. On the 8th of April, 1992, Mr. Ostojic gave an interview on Radio Belgrade. 1501. In Serbian, we are looking at the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And it says: "Just as inter-party talks began between representatives of the Serbian and Muslim peoples on delineating territory and separating organs of authority, in the Serbian territorials in a peaceful and democratic way a unit of the Muslim people attacked positions of the Serbian territories not far from Foca." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From the territory of Sukovac and that is a -- not far from the municipality, perhaps some 100 metres as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now the first sentence: "On behalf of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian people in the Foca commune, we are calling on citizens of all nationalities in Foca to remain calm because" -- and so on and so forth. Was any such appeal sent out to people?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From me personally and from Mr. Lojo Taib, the president of the municipality, it aired on the radio. It was a four-sentence long communique. If you wish I can read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Taib Lojo is what by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Muslim. He was at the Muslim representative of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3319, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to call up the next document, but similar things are repeated in P3338 issued on the 14th of April. Also Mr. Ostojic sent a report to Radio Belgrade. We don't have the time to call this up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mladjenovic, a statement was read to you by a witness who testified under pseudonym about rallies and what was said at those rallies. First of all, tell us this: Were those rallies accessible to the media and to journalists?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, both. Journalists had access to both if you have in mind the Serbian ones in 1990 and 1991. But the same is true of the Muslim rallies. They were widely covered by the media. I have that videotape, the promotion of the Serbian Democratic Party. Unfortunately, I could not get hold of the Muslim audio recording because I had to check some of the sentences. I did not want to mislead the Trial Chamber, the Prosecution and the Defence -- and give them something that is not correct. In any case, everything was recorded by camera and by tape recorder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When it comes to the media, was the allegedly drastic sentence academician Maksimovic highlighted in the media? Was any other war mongering, chauvinist statement conveyed from those rallies?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you this: As far as I can remember, if anything like that was uttered, it could have been in the shape of a warning based on various experiences, both of the Muslim and the Serbian peoples from the previous wars. I believe that Mr. Kilibarda uttered some harsher words. Mr. Muhamed Cengic, who was a Muslim, was very moderate in his appearance. So I really did not see anything. Mr. Karadzic is absolutely, in favour of living together in the former Yugoslavia. And other speakers who were more or less of a minor importance at that first rally. Before the elections after the SDS was set up in 1990. And then the tripartite rally in 1991 also saw appearances by speakers who presented very similar things. At the SDA rally, when the SDA was set up in 1992 I did not attend that for personal reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That witness who said that academician Maksimovic uttered those drastic words, was he telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who you are talking about, but I can assume that he was not telling the truth. Or at least not the whole truth. Everything can be spined in different ways. But he is a bit short-tempered in real life but he did not embark on that adventure. I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember if Mr. Muhamed Cengic, who was the vice-president of the SDA, and I and our teams paid homage to the victims of the Second World War? Did we do that in 1992 during the setting up of the SDS in Foca?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct you threw flowers from the bridge of the Drina across the street from the KP Dom. And also from the bridge on the Drina, the young people and children threw flowers into the river. I don't know which of the politicians were there. There was a lot of people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is impossible to catch up the speed in which both of you are speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Give us a short summary of what you just said. You said about throwing flowers, and in addition to the children who followed us, do you remember anybody else but Muhamed Filipovic and myself? We went to the bridge and threw flowers to pay homage to the victims of the Second World War. Do you remember who else was there?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that you misspoke, because Cengic was there. Muhamed Cengic and you and the children who followed you. Not Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I apologise, it was Cengic, yes. So how would it tally with the words that were ascribed to Professor Maksimovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The two don't together of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And my last question. Could you please tell us something about the leaflet that you mentioned in the cross-examination but you were not allowed to show it to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the usher please display it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that you have it at your disposal. The Defence has it, I'm sure. This is it. Only this part.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Whose the person who distributed the leaflets?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA MLADJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the August rally in 1990, when the SDA was promoted as a party, that leaflet was distributed among the people and you see who the promotion was dedicated to. It was Sabanovic from Visegrad who participated in the destruction of the bus. Murat Sabanovic was his name. He was the one who distributed it, the leaflets. Look at the contents and it will be self-explanatory indeed. How shall I put it? I was the consumer. Somebody would ring my bell late at night and then I couldn't go back to sleep, and so on and so forth. But you can read the thing for yourself and then you can see how welcome as neighbours we were to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Bells would be rung late. Children should be prohibited to play with the Serbian children. Garbage should be left in front of the doors. People should urinate in front of doors. Newspapers should not be delivered.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
